rw: Acceptance is the offeree's unqualified agreement to the exact terms of the offer, which is what turns an offer into a binding contract under the mirror image rule.

ww.A request for more time to decide on it: Asking for more time is only a request or delay, not agreement, so the offer stays open or lapses and no contract has formed yet.
ww.A refusal to deal with the other side: Refusing to deal is a rejection, which ends the offer completely and creates no contract, because acceptance requires agreeing rather than turning the offer down.
ww.A counter proposal with changed terms: A counter proposal with changed terms is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer and starts a new one instead of accepting it.

rw: Changing the price from $200 to $150 is a counteroffer, which acts as a rejection of the original offer and lets Lena accept or decline the new terms.

ww.A promise to pay the full price later on: Sam does not promise to pay the full price later; he states a lower price of $150, so his reply changes the terms rather than agreeing to them.
ww.A binding contract at a price of $175 to: No contract exists at $175 or any price yet, because Sam named $150 and Lena has not agreed to anything, so there is no meeting of the minds.
ww.An acceptance of the original asking pri: Sam did not accept the $200 asking price, since acceptance must match the offer exactly, and offering $150 instead is a different proposal altogether.

rw: A minor, usually someone under 18, lacks full capacity, so the contract is generally voidable by the minor, who can cancel it to protect young people from bad deals.

ww.A lawyer: A lawyer is an adult of full legal age and sound mind, so a lawyer has the capacity to make binding contracts like any other competent person.
ww.An adult: An adult of sound mind generally has full capacity to contract, so an ordinary adult can be bound by the agreements he or she signs.
ww.A company: A company is a legal entity that can contract through its authorized agents, so it has capacity and can be bound by agreements it makes.

rw: Fraud or duress defeats genuine consent, since one party was deceived or forced, which makes the contract void or voidable at the harmed party's choice.

ww.A signing on Monday: The day of the week a contract is signed has no effect on validity, because contracts can be formed on any day, so Monday is not a legal defect.
ww.A long contract: Length does not affect validity, since long contracts are enforceable if they meet the requirements, and a lengthy document is not a legal defect in itself.
ww.The use of blue ink: The color of ink used to sign has no legal effect, because courts care about real agreement and proper formation, never about the pen used.

rw: A void contract, such as one for an illegal purpose, has no legal effect from the start, while a voidable contract is valid until the protected party chooses to cancel it.

ww.Both kinds are always fully enforceable: Void and voidable contracts are not both enforceable, because a void contract has no legal effect at all and a voidable one can be canceled.
ww.A void contract can be canceled by eithe: This reverses the idea: a void contract is invalid from the start and cannot be ratified, while the voidable one is the contract that can be canceled.
ww.Both kinds must be in writing and signed: Neither kind needs a notary, and only certain contracts must be in writing under the Statute of Frauds, so this does not describe void or voidable contracts.

rw: Duress is improper pressure or threats that force someone to sign, so consent is not voluntary and the contract is voidable by the victim.

ww.Honest negotiation between the two parti: Honest negotiation in good faith is the normal, lawful way to reach agreement, whereas duress involves threats or pressure that remove a person's free choice.
ww.Reading a contract carefully before sign: Reading a contract carefully with a lawyer is smart practice that supports informed consent, which is the opposite of being forced to agree.
ww.A deadline that the other party has set: Setting a payment deadline is an ordinary contract term and is not a threat, so it does not take away anyone's free will to agree.

rw: Undue influence happens when someone in a position of trust, like a caregiver or advisor, unfairly sways a person, so the agreement may be voidable.

ww.Offering a fair discount on the price of: A fair discount is a legitimate pricing choice that gives the buyer a real benefit, so it involves no abuse of trust or unfair pressure.
ww.Advertising a product in an honest way t: Honest advertising informs customers truthfully, so it is lawful and does not take advantage of a trusting relationship to override anyone's free judgment.
ww.Meeting a deadline set in the contract o: Meeting a contract deadline on time is simply performing a duty as agreed, and it has nothing to do with unfair pressure over another's decision.

rw: Misrepresentation is a false statement of material fact that persuades someone to enter a contract, which can make the contract voidable by the misled party.

ww.A request for payment of an overdue bill: A request for payment of an overdue bill is a collection notice about an existing debt, and it makes no false statement that induces a contract.
ww.A truthful description of what a product: A truthful description is honest, so it cannot mislead anyone, while misrepresentation requires a false statement of fact that influences the other party.
ww.A statement of the seller's own opinion: An opinion is not a statement of fact, so a seller's own opinion is generally not misrepresentation, and is closer to puffery than to false facts.

rw: Puffery is exaggerated sales talk, like saying a pizza is the best ever, that reasonable buyers do not take as fact, so it creates no liability.

ww.A written warranty that comes with a pro: A written warranty is a specific promise about a product that can be enforced, whereas puffery is only vague sales talk that creates no legal duty.
ww.A refund policy posted in the store wind: A posted refund policy is a concrete store term that customers may rely on, while puffery is vague boasting that nobody treats as a specific promise.
ww.A fraudulent claim about measurable prod: A fraudulent claim about measurable facts can be misrepresentation or fraud, whereas puffery is harmless exaggeration that no reasonable person takes literally.

rw: The Statute of Frauds requires certain kinds of contracts, such as land sales and promises that last over a year, to be in writing to be enforceable.

ww.Contracts to be filed with the local pol: Contracts are not filed with police to be enforceable, and the Statute of Frauds concerns written evidence of certain agreements rather than any police filing.
ww.All contracts to last for at least a yea: Not all contracts must last a year or more, since most are short and valid, and the rule applies only to certain contract types that need a writing.
ww.All contracts to be notarized by a notar: Notarization is not generally required by the Statute of Frauds, which asks for a signed writing for certain contracts, not a notary's seal on all of them.

rw: Contracts for the sale of land or real estate interests fall within the Statute of Frauds, so they must generally be in writing and signed to be enforceable.

ww.A contract to share a school ride: A casual agreement to share a ride to school is a small everyday deal that does not fall in a Statute of Frauds category, so an oral promise can work.
ww.A contract to buy a sandwich today: A same-day sandwich purchase is a small sale of goods under the $500 UCC threshold, and it is completed at once, so it needs no writing.
ww.A contract to borrow a pencil: Borrowing a pencil is a trivial informal arrangement that no Statute of Frauds category covers, so it can be made orally and still be binding.

rw: A breach occurs when a party fails to perform a duty the contract requires, whether by not performing at all, performing late, or performing badly.

ww.Reading the contract carefully before si: Reading a contract carefully is part of good diligence before signing and is not a breach, because breach means failing to do what the contract requires.
ww.Completing all of the duties on time as: Completing all duties on time is full performance, which is the opposite of breach, since a breach occurs only when a promised duty goes unfulfilled.
ww.Negotiating the terms before signing the: Negotiating terms before signing is a normal part of contract formation, and since no contract exists yet there is nothing that could be breached.

rw: Money damages are the most common remedy, paying the injured party enough to cover the loss caused by the breach and put them where performance would have.

ww.Loss of rights: Loss of rights is not the usual remedy for breach, because courts normally compensate the injured party rather than strip a person of legal rights.
ww.Prison time: Prison time is for crimes, and breach of contract is a civil wrong, so a person generally cannot be jailed for failing to perform a private contract.
ww.Automatic arrest: Automatic arrest does not follow breach, because contract disputes are civil matters settled in court with remedies like damages, not through the police.

rw: Specific performance is a court order that forces the breaching party to carry out the contract as promised, used when money alone cannot fix the harm.

ww.A court decision to cancel the whole con: Canceling the whole contract is rescission, which undoes the deal, whereas specific performance does the opposite by requiring the contract to be carried out.
ww.A penalty that is paid to the state when: A penalty paid to the state is a fine, which is not a contract remedy, because contract remedies compensate the injured party and do not punish the wrongdoer.
ww.A court order to pay punitive damages to: Punitive damages are money awards meant to punish, and they are rare in contract cases, while specific performance orders actual performance instead of payment.

rw: Unique items like a rare painting or a parcel of land cannot be replaced by money, so a court may order the seller to deliver the exact item.

ww.For ordinary goods that are easily bough: Ordinary goods easily bought elsewhere can be replaced with money damages, so courts see no need to force the seller to perform in those cases.
ww.For routine office supplies bought every: Routine office supplies are common items available from many stores, so a buyer can simply buy substitutes and collect the cost difference as damages.
ww.For any contract at all, whatever the su: Courts do not order specific performance for any contract at all, because it is an exceptional remedy used only when damages are inadequate for the subject matter.

rw: Rescission cancels a contract and returns both parties to where they were before it was made, often used for fraud, mistake or duress.

ww.Extending the deadline in the contract f: Extending a payment deadline is a modification of the contract that keeps the deal alive, whereas rescission cancels the deal and undoes it.
ww.Transferring the contract over to someon: Transferring a contract to someone else is an assignment or delegation, which keeps the contract in force, unlike rescission, which ends it.
ww.Doubling the price stated in the written: Doubling the stated price would change the terms and would need both parties' agreement, and it has nothing to do with canceling a contract.

rw: To assign a contract is to transfer one's rights under it to another person, called the assignee, who can then collect the benefits owed.

ww.To change the price stated in the contra: Changing the price is a modification of the contract's terms, which generally needs both parties to agree, and it is not what assigning means.
ww.To cancel the whole contract entirely fo: Canceling a contract entirely is rescission or termination, while assignment keeps the contract alive and only changes who holds the rights under it.
ww.To sue the other party for damages in co: Suing the other party for damages is a remedy for breach, which is a different legal step from assigning a contract to a third party.

rw: The UCC is a uniform set of state laws governing commercial transactions, especially the sale and lease of goods, payment instruments, and secured lending.

ww.Criminal punishments for crimes of theft: Criminal punishments for theft come from state criminal codes, while the UCC covers commercial dealings such as sales, leases, and negotiable instruments.
ww.Zoning of land inside a city or a town a: Zoning is controlled by local land-use ordinances and municipal governments, not by the UCC, which regulates commercial sales and related business transactions.
ww.Immigration rules for foreign workers in: Immigration rules for foreign workers are set by federal immigration law, whereas the UCC deals with commercial transactions such as sales and secured loans.

rw: Article 2 of the UCC governs the sale of goods, meaning movable tangible items such as cars, computers and furniture, and it sets default sales rules.

ww.The sale of land: Land is real property, which falls under real estate law and the Statute of Frauds, not Article 2, which covers only movable goods.
ww.Employment agreements: Employment agreements are governed by contract and labor law, since Article 2 covers goods rather than agreements for personal work or services.
ww.Haircut services: A haircut is a service, not a good, so common law contract rules apply to it instead of the UCC's sales article.

rw: Fifty laptops are tangible, movable goods, so buying them is a sale of goods that falls under UCC Article 2 and its warranty and delivery rules.

ww.A contract to lease an apartment: A lease of an apartment is real property, which is governed by landlord-tenant and common law rules, and Article 2 does not apply to real estate.
ww.A contract to buy a house: A house is real property, so its sale falls under real estate law, while Article 2 applies only to sales of movable goods.
ww.A contract to hire a tutor: Hiring a tutor is a contract for services rather than goods, so general common law contract rules apply and Article 2 does not.

rw: The UCC lets merchants form a contract even with open terms, as long as they intended to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for relief.

ww.Only if every single term is agreed by b: The UCC does not demand that every term be settled, because gap fillers supply missing terms, so merchants do not need full agreement on every detail.
ww.Only after a court has approved the cont: Court approval is not needed to form a contract, since parties create contracts by their own agreement, and courts only get involved if there is a dispute.
ww.Only when a lawyer is present at the sig: A lawyer's presence is not required to form a contract, because valid contracts between merchants can be made by phone, email or handshake.

rw: Under the UCC Statute of Frauds, a sale of goods for $500 or more generally needs a writing signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought.

ww.A notary public and two outside witnesse: A notary and witnesses are not required for a UCC sale, which asks only for a signed writing for goods priced at $500 or more.
ww.A government stamp on every page of the: No government stamp is needed on contracts, and the UCC's formal requirement is a simple signed writing rather than any official mark or seal.
ww.Court approval that is granted before th: A court never has to approve a sale before it happens, since parties may contract freely, and courts only step in after a dispute arises.

rw: An express warranty is a specific promise or description by the seller about the goods, which can be spoken, written, or shown by sample, that becomes part of the deal.

ww.A refusal to cover any defects in the go: Refusing to cover defects describes a disclaimer, which limits warranties, while an express warranty is an affirmative promise that the goods meet certain terms.
ww.A promise that the law implies automatic: A promise the law implies automatically in every sale describes an implied warranty, but an express warranty is one the seller states directly.
ww.A tax that is charged on sales made by a: A sales tax is a government charge on purchases and is unrelated to warranties, which are promises about the quality or features of goods.

rw: The implied warranty of merchantability means goods sold by a merchant are fit for their ordinary purpose, are of fair average quality, and are properly labeled.

ww.Goods will never lose any of their value: No seller guarantees that goods will never lose value, since market value changes, and merchantability concerns basic quality rather than future price.
ww.Goods will be delivered within a single: Delivery timing is a matter of the contract terms, and merchantability concerns the quality of the goods rather than how quickly they arrive.
ww.Goods will be sold only at a discount to: Selling at a discount is a pricing decision and has no link to quality, while merchantability promises ordinary fitness regardless of the price paid.

rw: This warranty arises when the seller knows the buyer's particular purpose and the buyer relies on the seller's skill to select goods suited to that need.

ww.The goods come with a free yearly mainte: A free yearly maintenance plan would be an express service promise, whereas the fitness warranty is implied by law when special needs are known.
ww.The goods can be returned for absolutely: Returns for any reason are a store policy and are not part of a fitness warranty, which depends on the buyer's reliance on the seller's expertise.
ww.The goods are always provided free of ch: Goods are not required to be free, since a warranty about suitability for a purpose has nothing to do with the price the buyer pays.

rw: Selling a product as is means the seller disclaims implied warranties, so the buyer accepts the goods in their current condition, defects and all.

ww.The price is free of any charge for buye: As is describes the condition of the goods, not the price, so an item sold as is can still be sold at full price.
ww.The buyer may return the goods in a mont: As is sales generally do not offer a return period, and any return right would have to come from a separate promise by the seller.
ww.The seller guarantees perfect quality: As is is the opposite of a guarantee, because the seller refuses to promise any quality, so perfect quality is never assured.

rw: Title is legal ownership of the goods, and it matters because it determines who may sell the goods, who can claim them, and when risk passes.

ww.A name printed on the box: A name on the box is branding or labeling and shows nothing about who legally owns the goods, which is what title means.
ww.A fee charged for the goods: A fee for the goods is a price, which is a payment term and is different from the legal ownership that title represents.
ww.The seller's street address: The seller's street address is just contact information and has no bearing on the question of who legally owns the goods.

rw: Risk of loss decides which party, buyer or seller, bears the financial loss if goods are damaged, stolen or destroyed before the sale is complete.

ww.The chance that a buyer will change thei: A buyer changing their mind is a matter of cancellation or contract rights, whereas risk of loss concerns who pays when goods are damaged or destroyed.
ww.The profit margin that the seller earns: Profit margin is the seller's earnings on a sale, which is an accounting concept and is not related to who bears loss from damaged goods.
ww.A fee that is charged for insurance cove: An insurance fee is a cost of coverage, but risk of loss allocates responsibility for damage and does not mean a charge for insurance.

rw: Under F.O.B. shipping point the buyer bears the risk of loss once the seller hands the goods to the carrier, and typically pays the freight cost too.

ww.The seller bears all shipping risk until: Under F.O.B. shipping point the risk moves to the buyer at shipment, so the seller does not keep the risk until the buyer pays in full.
ww.The goods are provided free of charge to: F.O.B. here means free on board, not free of charge, so the buyer still pays the purchase price for the goods.
ww.The buyer pays no shipping costs at all,: F.O.B. shipping point does not mean the seller covers shipping, since the buyer normally pays freight, and the term mainly allocates risk and shipping costs to the buyer.

rw: With F.O.B. destination the seller bears the risk of loss and usually pays shipping until the goods arrive at the buyer's location.

ww.The buyer bears the risk from the factor: The buyer bearing risk from the factory door describes F.O.B. shipping point, while destination terms keep the risk on the seller during transit.
ww.The goods are free on board for every si: F.O.B. stands for free on board, which names the point where risk passes, so it does not mean the goods are free to every buyer.
ww.The goods never actually leave the wareh: Goods under F.O.B. destination do get shipped to the buyer, so the term has nothing to do with them staying in the warehouse.

rw: A negotiable instrument, such as a check or promissory note, is a signed written promise or order to pay that can be transferred to another person.

ww.A court order that requires one party to: A court order to pay damages is a judgment and not a negotiable instrument, which is a payment document that can be transferred to others.
ww.A receipt that is given for goods bought: A receipt only proves a purchase and contains no unconditional promise to pay money, so it cannot be a negotiable instrument.
ww.A free gift certificate that is given ou: A gift certificate is a store credit redeemed for goods and is not an unconditional promise to pay a sum of money to its holder.

rw: A promissory note is a written promise by one person to pay another a definite sum of money, either on demand or at a set date.

ww.A list of all of the unpaid bills owed: A list of unpaid bills is a record of accounts payable, not a promise to pay, so it lacks the signed promise of a note.
ww.A receipt that is given for a payment ma: A receipt confirms that a payment has been made, while a promissory note is a promise to pay in the future.
ww.A written order to a bank to pay a perso: A written order to a bank to pay a person describes a check, which is an order, whereas a promissory note is a direct promise.

rw: A check is a written order from the drawer telling a bank to pay a specific sum to the payee or to the bearer on demand.

ww.A promise by a bank to lend money later: A bank lending money later describes a loan commitment, but a check is the account holder's order for the bank to pay from existing funds.
ww.A contract between the bank and the paye: A check is not a contract between the bank and the payee; it is an order from the drawer, so the payee has no direct agreement with the bank.
ww.A receipt that is issued for cash: A receipt only confirms that cash was received, and a check is a different document because it orders a bank to pay money.

rw: The drawer is the person who writes and signs the check, ordering the bank to pay money out of the drawer's account.

ww.The person who endorses the check later: The person who endorses the check is the endorser, usually the payee, who signs the back to transfer it or deposit it, not the drawer.
ww.The bank that finally pays the check: The bank that pays the check is the drawee, since it is the party ordered to pay, so it is not the drawer.
ww.The person who receives the money from i: The person who receives the money is the payee, because the payee is named on the check as the one entitled to payment.

rw: The payee is the person or business named on the check as the one to be paid, and that name is written on the payee line.

ww.The clerk who prints the blank check for: The clerk who prints blank checks has no role in the transaction, and the payee is the person named on the check to receive the money.
ww.The bank that holds the check writer's f: The bank that holds the check writer's funds is the drawee, since it is the one ordered to pay the check.
ww.The person who signs the check as the wr: The person who signs the check as the writer is the drawer, who is the one paying, whereas the payee is the one receiving.

rw: An endorsement is a signature, often on the back of a check, that transfers the payee's rights to someone else or authorizes depositing it.

ww.A bank fee that is charged for cashing a: A bank fee for cashing a check is a service charge, while an endorsement is a signature that transfers or deposits the check.
ww.A copy of the check that is kept for the: A copy kept for records is a duplicate or register entry, but an endorsement is a signature on the back of the instrument itself.
ww.A promise to repay a loan at some later: A promise to repay a loan is a promissory note, which is a separate document, and has nothing to do with signing the back of a check.

rw: A blank endorsement is just the payee's signature, which turns the check into bearer paper payable to whoever holds it, so it should be signed with care.

ww.An endorsement that says 'for deposit on: An endorsement reading for deposit only is a restrictive endorsement, which limits how the check may be used rather than leaving it open to anyone.
ww.An endorsement that names one specific n: Naming one specific new payee is a special endorsement, which directs payment to that named person, so it is not the blank kind.
ww.A missing signature on the back of the c: A blank endorsement is not a missing signature, because it contains the signature, and the check is not stopped from moving by it.

rw: A restrictive endorsement limits how the check can be used, as with for deposit only, so the funds can only go into the named account.

ww.A signature that lets the check pass to: A signature that lets the check pass to anyone is a blank endorsement, which makes the check payable to the holder, not a restricted one.
ww.A signature that names one specific new: A signature naming one specific new payee is a special endorsement, which directs payment to that person, and it does not restrict the use.
ww.A flat refusal to sign the back of the c: Refusing to sign means no endorsement exists, so the check cannot be properly negotiated, and it is not a type of endorsement at all.

rw: Non-sufficient funds means the drawer's account did not hold enough money to cover the check, so the bank refuses to pay it and returns it.

ww.The check was written in the wrong color: Ink color has no bearing on whether a check clears, since banks reject checks for funds problems or other defects, not for the pen used.
ww.The bank closed the payee's account last: The message concerns the drawer's account balance, not the payee's account, so a closed payee account would not produce an NSF return.
ww.The payee forgot to endorse the back of: A missing endorsement is a different problem that would be flagged separately, and NSF refers only to the writer's account lacking funds.

rw: A secured transaction is a loan backed by collateral, so if the borrower defaults the lender can claim the pledged property to recover the debt.

ww.A cash sale with no paperwork or documen: A cash sale with no paperwork has no collateral or security agreement, so it is the opposite of a secured transaction.
ww.A transaction the government guarantees: Government guarantees against loss describe loan guarantee programs or insured deposits, but a secured transaction is secured by collateral the lender can take.
ww.A loan that has no repayment required of: A loan requiring no repayment is a gift or grant, and a secured transaction still requires repayment, with collateral as backup security.

rw: Collateral is property, such as a car or a house, that a borrower pledges to secure a loan, and the lender may take it if the loan goes unpaid.

ww.A fee charged by a lender or bank: A fee charged by a lender is interest or a service charge, whereas collateral is property pledged to back the loan.
ww.A refund for early repayment of debt: A refund for early repayment of debt is a rebate or a prepayment benefit, not collateral, which is pledged property.
ww.A verbal promise that has no property: A verbal promise with no property attached gives the lender nothing to claim, so it cannot serve as collateral securing the loan.

rw: A security interest is a lender's legal claim on collateral, which lets the lender take and sell the property if the borrower defaults on the loan.

ww.A guard hired to protect a store or bank: A guard protects property and has nothing to do with the lender's legal right to take collateral, which is what a security interest means.
ww.An interest rate on savings accounts: An interest rate on savings is the return a depositor earns, but a security interest is a lender's claim on property.
ww.A refund of interest paid on loans: A refund of interest paid is a rebate to the borrower, but a security interest gives the lender rights in the borrower's property.

rw: Perfecting a security interest means taking a step such as filing a financing statement so the lender's claim is effective against other creditors and buyers.

ww.To sell the collateral to a new buyer fo: Selling collateral to a new buyer would remove the lender's security rather than perfect it, and perfection is about the lender's priority.
ww.To repay the whole loan in full right aw: Repaying the loan in full would end the debt and the security interest, not perfect it, because perfection protects a lender with an unpaid loan.
ww.To make the collateral completely flawle: Perfection has nothing to do with the physical or market quality of the collateral, because it is a legal step that protects the lender's claim.

rw: A UCC-1 financing statement is a public filing that gives notice of a lender's security interest in collateral, which helps perfect the interest and set priority.

ww.A receipt that is issued for collateral: A receipt for collateral would only confirm that property was received, while a financing statement is a public filing that gives notice of the lender's claim.
ww.A company's yearly income statement repo: A yearly income statement is an accounting report of revenues and expenses, and it has nothing to do with filing notice of a lender's claim.
ww.A bank statement showing deposits to an: A bank statement lists deposits and withdrawals on an account, whereas a UCC-1 is a public notice of a security interest in the debtor's property.

rw: Upon default a secured lender may repossess the collateral and usually sell it, following the law, to apply the proceeds to the unpaid debt.

ww.Take all of the borrower's other propert: A secured lender's rights are generally limited to the pledged collateral, so the lender cannot just take the borrower's other unrelated property.
ww.Ignore the debt and simply wait for paym: Simply ignoring the debt is not a required response, since the lender has remedies, and a secured creditor can act on its security interest.
ww.Destroy the borrower's records and files: Destroying a borrower's records is unlawful and is no remedy at all, because a secured lender must follow legal procedures when it enforces its rights.

rw: Employment at will means either the employer or the employee can end the job at any time for any lawful reason, with or without notice, in most states.

ww.Employers must give a reason and a year': At will employment does not require a stated reason or a year's notice, because the arrangement lets either side end it freely, within legal limits.
ww.Employees must stay for a minimum of one: There is no minimum stay required of employees, since an at will worker may resign at any time, and only a contract could set a term.
ww.Employees can only be fired after a writ: At will employees do not need a written warning before dismissal, since the employer may end the job without a progressive discipline process, unless a contract says otherwise.

rw: The FLSA sets the federal minimum wage, requires overtime pay for covered employees working over 40 hours a week, and restricts child labor.

ww.Taxes that are charged on business profi: Business profit taxes are set by tax laws such as the Internal Revenue Code, while the FLSA covers wages, hours and child labor.
ww.Rules for owning and running a franchise: Franchise rules come from franchise regulations and contract law, but the FLSA is a labor law about wages and hours of employees.
ww.Standards for how products are packaged: Packaging and labeling standards are covered by consumer protection and product safety laws, not by the FLSA, which regulates pay and employment conditions.

rw: Overtime pay is extra pay, often 1.5 times the regular rate, owed to non-exempt employees for hours worked beyond 40 in a week.

ww.Pay that is given for training sessions: Training pay may be due under wage rules, but overtime pay specifically means higher pay for hours beyond the weekly limit.
ww.Pay that is given for sick days taken at: Sick day pay is a benefit set by employer policy or state law, and it is different from overtime pay for hours beyond 40.
ww.A bonus that is paid once every year to: An annual bonus is extra compensation paid once a year at the employer's choice, which is not tied to hours worked over 40.

rw: Exempt employees, often salaried executives or professionals, are not entitled to overtime pay, while non-exempt employees must receive it for hours beyond 40.

ww.Exempt employees must work overtime for: Exempt employees are not forced to work overtime for free; they simply are not entitled to overtime pay, which is paid to non-exempt workers.
ww.Exempt employees pay no taxes on their w: Both exempt and non-exempt employees must pay taxes on wages, so exempt status refers to overtime rules and not to tax treatment.
ww.There is no difference between the two g: There is a real legal difference, because exemption decides whether the FLSA overtime rules apply, so the two groups are treated differently.

rw: Overtime is 1.5 times $14, which is $21 per hour, and the 5 hours over 40 are paid at $21, so 5 times $21 equals $105.

ww.$70 for the 5 extra hours at $14 per hou: This pays the extra hours at straight time of $14, which is wrong because overtime must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate.
ww.$0 because the job is hourly, not salari: Hourly workers who are non-exempt are owed overtime, so the job being hourly does not remove the right to overtime pay at all.
ww.$140 for the 5 extra hours at $28 per ho: This uses double the regular rate, $28, but the FLSA requires time and a half, so 5 hours at $28 equals $140, which is too high.

rw: The Equal Pay Act prohibits paying men and women different wages for equal work in jobs requiring equal skill, effort and responsibility at the same place.

ww.Paying any worker more than the minimum: The act does not limit how much a worker can earn above minimum wage, and it targets pay differences based on sex.
ww.Paying bonuses to high-performing worker: The Equal Pay Act does not ban bonuses for strong performers, since pay differences based on merit are allowed, but not those based on sex.
ww.Paying workers on a weekly pay schedule: The Equal Pay Act does not cover pay schedules, as employers can choose weekly or other pay periods, and it focuses on equal pay.

rw: Title VII bans job discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and it covers hiring, firing, pay and other employment terms.

ww.Requiring all employees to wear company: Requiring uniforms is a normal workplace policy and not discrimination, so Title VII does not prohibit employers from setting dress rules.
ww.Offering paid vacation days to employees: Offering paid vacation is a lawful employee benefit, and Title VII does not prohibit it, though it does require benefits to be offered without discrimination.
ww.Hiring workers only if they are under th: Hiring only people under 40 would be age discrimination, which another law, the ADEA, prohibits, and it is not what Title VII bans.

rw: The ADEA protects workers and applicants age 40 and older from age-based discrimination in hiring, firing, pay and other terms of employment.

ww.Only government employees: The ADEA covers private employers and others, not only government employees, so limiting it to public workers misstates its reach.
ww.Only retired workers: The ADEA is not limited to retirees, since it protects people who are still working or applying for jobs, as long as they are old enough.
ww.Workers under 18 only: Workers under 18 are covered by child labor rules, while the ADEA protects older workers, which means those age 40 and above.

rw: The ADA requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations, such as modified equipment or schedules, so qualified workers with disabilities can do essential job duties.

ww.Lower standards for every task in the jo: The ADA does not lower standards for tasks, since employees must still perform the essential functions of the job, with or without accommodation.
ww.A guaranteed promotion for every disable: The ADA does not guarantee promotions, because disabled workers are treated like others and must be qualified for advancement just as any worker is.
ww.Free housing for all of the disabled wor: Employers are not required to provide housing, because accommodations relate to doing the job, such as adjusted equipment or schedules, not living arrangements.

rw: A screen reader helps an employee with low vision do the essential job duties, which makes it a typical reasonable accommodation under the ADA.

ww.Paying a special bonus because of the di: A special bonus tied to disability is not an accommodation, because accommodations help an employee perform the job and are not extra pay.
ww.Removing all of the employee's required: Removing all required duties would eliminate the job itself, and the ADA does not require employers to remove essential functions of the position.
ww.Lowering the employee's pay to cover the: Cutting pay to cover accommodation costs is illegal, since employers must pay the cost of reasonable accommodations and cannot pass it to the worker.

rw: The FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per year for family and medical reasons, like childbirth or serious illness.

ww.A guaranteed raise after the leave ends: The FMLA does not promise a raise after leave, though it does protect the employee's right to return to the same or an equivalent job.
ww.Unlimited paid leave for every single wo: The FMLA does not give unlimited paid leave, since it provides a limited amount of leave that is unpaid, though employees may use paid leave if available.
ww.Paid leave lasting a full year for every: The FMLA does not provide a full year of paid leave, because the maximum is generally 12 weeks of unpaid leave.

rw: Sexual harassment is unwelcome sexual conduct, including advances or comments, that creates a hostile work environment or is tied to employment decisions.

ww.Giving honest feedback about someone's w: Honest feedback about work is a normal part of management and is not harassment, since harassment involves unwelcome sexual conduct or sex-based hostility.
ww.Wearing a company uniform to the office: Wearing a company uniform is a dress policy and is not harassment, because harassment involves unwelcome behavior, which a uniform rule is not.
ww.Friendly teamwork on a shared group proj: Friendly teamwork on a group project is welcome and professional conduct, so it differs from the unwelcome behavior that defines sexual harassment.

rw: Reporting harassment through the employer's complaint process puts the company on notice and starts an investigation, and it also helps protect the employee legally.

ww.Ignore it and simply hope that it all st: Ignoring the problem usually lets it continue and can weaken a later complaint, so employees are advised to act rather than hope it stops.
ww.Retaliate against the person harassing t: Retaliating against the harasser can create problems for the victim, who might face discipline, and it does not follow proper reporting procedures.
ww.Quit the job without telling anyone why: Quitting without telling anyone gives the employer no chance to fix the problem, and it can hurt later legal claims or benefits.

rw: Retaliation is punishing an employee, through firing, demotion or other harm, for reporting wrongdoing or exercising legal rights, and it is illegal.

ww.Reviewing an employee's work performance: An honest performance review is a legitimate management activity and is not retaliation unless it is a punishment for protected activity.
ww.Training new staff members on procedures: Training new staff on procedures is a normal duty of employers and has nothing to do with punishing someone for protected actions.
ww.Giving an employee a fair raise for good: A fair raise for good work is a reward based on merit, so it is the opposite of punishing someone for protected activity.

rw: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards through inspections, training and penalties.

ww.Regulates how the stock market operates: Stock market operation is overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission, not OSHA, which deals with workplace safety and health.
ww.Collects the income taxes owed by worker: Collecting income taxes is the job of the Internal Revenue Service, whereas OSHA concerns workplace safety and does not handle taxes.
ww.Sets the minimum wages that all employer: Minimum wage rules are set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Department of Labor's wage division, not by OSHA.

rw: OSHA requires employers to keep the workplace free from recognized hazards that could cause death or serious harm, under the General Duty Clause.

ww.Offer free meals to every worker on the: OSHA does not require meals for workers, because it is a safety agency whose rules deal with hazards and not with perks.
ww.Give all of its workers a company car to: Employers are not required by OSHA to give cars to workers, since its rules cover safe workplaces and not company benefits.
ww.Pay all of its employees exactly equal s: OSHA does not require equal salaries for all employees, because pay is regulated by wage laws, and its role is about safe working conditions.

rw: Workers' compensation is insurance that pays medical costs and part of lost wages for employees hurt or made ill on the job, no matter who was at fault.

ww.A tax that is charged on employee wages: A tax on wages is a payroll tax, but workers' compensation is an insurance system funded by employers for injured workers.
ww.A bonus that rewards high performance at: A performance bonus is extra pay for results, while workers' compensation provides benefits to workers injured on the job.
ww.A retirement account that is funded by t: A retirement account funded by the worker alone is a savings plan like an IRA, which is not injury insurance paid for by employers.

rw: Workers' compensation covers medical treatment and part of lost wages for employees hurt on the job, like the warehouse worker who broke an arm.

ww.Unemployment insurance: Unemployment insurance pays people who lose jobs through no fault of their own, and it does not cover injuries that occur at work.
ww.A sales tax refund: A sales tax refund returns tax paid on purchases and has no link to paying medical bills or wages after a workplace injury.
ww.Social Security pay: Social Security pay mainly covers retirement, long-term disability and survivor benefits, and it is not the first system for a workplace injury.

rw: Unemployment insurance gives temporary income to people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own, like a layoff, while they look for new work.

ww.Pay for workers who quit their jobs with: Workers who quit without notice generally do not qualify, because unemployment insurance is meant for people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
ww.A bonus that rewards a worker for findin: A bonus for finding a new job is not unemployment insurance, which pays temporary income while a worker is out of work.
ww.A loan that helps someone start a compan: A loan to start a company is business financing, but unemployment insurance gives money to people who lost jobs and are looking for work.

rw: The NLRA protects employees' rights to organize, join unions, and bargain collectively with employers, and it bars employers from interfering with these rights.

ww.The right to own a share of the company': The NLRA does not guarantee a stake in company stock or profits, because it protects the right to organize and bargain, not to own shares.
ww.A guaranteed salary for every worker in: The NLRA does not guarantee any salary, because pay is negotiated or set by the employer, and the law protects the bargaining process.
ww.The right to work a shorter four-day wee: The NLRA does not guarantee a shorter work week on full pay, since hours and pay are decided through bargaining, not set by the law.

rw: A labor union is an organized group of workers who bargain together with employers over pay, benefits, hours and working conditions.

ww.A group of company owners who meet regul: A group of company owners who meet regularly is a trade association or board, whereas a union is made up of workers.
ww.A type of insurance company for workers: A union is not an insurance company, as it is a group representing workers, though some unions may offer benefits to members.
ww.A government agency that hires workers d: A union is a private organization of workers and not a government agency, and it does not hire workers directly.

rw: Collective bargaining is the negotiation between an employer and a union representing workers over wages, hours, benefits and other terms of employment.

ww.A vote by shareholders to choose a new C: A shareholder vote to choose a CEO is corporate governance, which is a different process from negotiating employment terms with a union.
ww.Negotiation between two competing compan: Competing companies negotiating prices would be price fixing, which is illegal under antitrust laws, and it is not collective bargaining.
ww.A customer haggling with a seller over a: A customer haggling over a price is ordinary bargaining between individuals, but collective bargaining involves a union negotiating for a group of workers.

rw: A strike is a work stoppage by employees, usually union members, used to press demands for better pay, benefits or conditions.

ww.A hiring event held by an employer each: A hiring event is a recruiting activity by the employer, whereas a strike is employees refusing to work to press their demands.
ww.An annual evaluation of an employee's wo: An annual evaluation is a performance review by management, but a strike is a collective work stoppage organized by employees.
ww.A short company shutdown ordered by the: A short company shutdown ordered by owners would be a lockout or closure, since a strike is started by the workers.

rw: A lockout is when an employer keeps workers out of the workplace and blocks work during a labor dispute, as pressure in negotiations.

ww.A paid day off for all of the staff memb: A paid day off for all staff is a holiday or company benefit, but a lockout means the employer stops the work.
ww.A secure entry system for the doors of a: A secure entry system is a physical security device, which is a different meaning from the labor term lockout.
ww.A worker who suddenly quits the job and: A worker who quits is resigning, while a lockout is an action taken by the employer, not by the worker.

rw: A right-to-work law is a state law that forbids requiring employees to join a union or pay union dues as a condition of keeping a job.

ww.A law that bans all unions in the whole: Right-to-work laws do not ban unions, because workers can still organize, but they bar contracts that force workers to join or pay a union.
ww.A law that guarantees each person a stat: A right-to-work law does not guarantee anyone a state job, because the name refers to freedom from compulsory union membership.
ww.A law that requires unions at every firm: Right-to-work laws do the opposite of requiring unions, since they limit union security agreements so that membership cannot be required.

rw: IRCA requires employers to verify each new hire's identity and eligibility to work in the United States by completing Form I-9 for every new employee.

ww.Hire only people who are full citizens o: IRCA does not require hiring only citizens, because it prohibits knowingly hiring unauthorized workers while also banning discrimination based on citizenship status or origin.
ww.Reject any applicants who have accents o: Rejecting applicants because of accents would be discrimination, which IRCA forbids, since it bans national origin discrimination in hiring.
ww.Ask for the tax returns of every applica: Employers are not required to ask for tax returns, as IRCA focuses on documents proving identity and work authorization on Form I-9.

rw: E-Verify is an online system that lets employers confirm a new hire's eligibility to work in the United States by comparing Form I-9 data to government records.

ww.A background check on credit scores and: A credit score and address check is a background screening, which is different from E-Verify, a system that checks work authorization.
ww.A system that sets the pay rates for all: E-Verify does not set pay rates, because it is a government work eligibility tool, and pay is set by employers and wage laws.
ww.A tool that businesses use for filing ta: Filing taxes is handled through IRS systems, and E-Verify is for checking whether new hires are authorized to work.

rw: An independent contractor is self-employed and controls how the work is done, and is paid per job instead of receiving wages as an employee.

ww.A full-time worker who receives benefits: A full-time worker with benefits is the usual description of an employee, and an independent contractor generally does not get employer benefits.
ww.A person serving a four-week probation p: A probation period is a trial stage for a new employee and has no link to being a self-employed contractor.
ww.A manager who works inside a company off: A manager working inside a company office is typically an employee, whereas an independent contractor is in business for themself.

rw: Control over when, where and how the work is done points to an employee, because employers direct employees, but contractors direct themselves.

ww.The worker uses their own tools and sets: Using their own tools and setting their own hours suggests an independent contractor, since employees typically use the employer's tools and follow its schedule.
ww.The worker serves many different clients: Serving many clients at once suggests a contractor who runs their own business, while employees usually work for one employer.
ww.The worker sends invoices for each proje: Sending invoices for each project is typical of contractors, who are paid per job, whereas employees are paid wages on payroll.

rw: A non-compete agreement is a contract in which an employee agrees not to work for competitors or start a rival business for a set time after leaving.

ww.A rule that sets the number of vacation: Vacation days are a benefit and policy matter, and a non-compete agreement is instead a contract restricting competition after the job ends.
ww.A promise that the employee will never q: A non-compete does not promise the employee will never quit, because it limits where they may work afterward, not whether they may leave.
ww.A guarantee that the employee gets a rai: A guarantee of yearly raises is a pay term, and a non-compete agreement instead deals with working for competitors after leaving.

rw: An NDA is a contract in which a person agrees to keep certain information, such as trade secrets or client lists, confidential and not to share it.

ww.A contract for a loan from a bank to a s: A bank loan contract involves borrowing and repayment, which is unrelated to an NDA, a contract used to protect secret information.
ww.A promise to work overtime when asked by: A promise to work overtime is a scheduling agreement and not an NDA, which deals with keeping certain information secret.
ww.A contract to share all company data wit: Sharing all company data with the public is the opposite of an NDA, which restricts disclosure of confidential information.

rw: A probationary period is an initial time when an employer evaluates a new employee's performance and fit for the job before making the position permanent.

ww.A period when the employee pays the comp: Employees do not pay the company to be on probation, and the period is simply a trial time when a new hire is evaluated.
ww.A period when the company is unable to f: Probation does not stop the company from firing anyone, and in many cases it is easier for an employer to end employment during it.
ww.A guaranteed contract that runs for five: A guaranteed five-year contract is a fixed-term employment contract, and probation is instead a short initial evaluation period.

rw: Wrongful termination is firing an employee for an illegal reason, such as discrimination, retaliation, or breach of contract, which can lead to a lawsuit.

ww.Laying off workers due to budget cuts: Layoffs due to budget cuts are legal business decisions based on economic conditions, not unlawful terminations, if done without discrimination.
ww.Firing for repeated lateness and no excu: Firing for repeated lateness with no excuse is a legitimate, lawful reason related to job performance, so it is not wrongful termination.
ww.Ending a probationary period for poor wo: Ending a probationary period for poor work is a lawful decision based on performance, so it does not count as wrongful termination.

rw: Firing a worker soon after a safety report to OSHA suggests retaliation, an illegal punishment for protected activity, and the timing supports that claim.

ww.Defamation: Defamation involves false statements that harm someone's reputation, which does not fit a firing that came right after a safety complaint.
ww.Breach of duty: Breach of duty is a negligence concept, while the key fact here is the firing right after a protected report, which points to retaliation.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an antitrust violation involving competitors agreeing on prices, and it has no connection to firing an employee.

rw: A layoff is a termination caused by business conditions such as budget cuts or reduced demand, not by the employee's own misconduct or performance.

ww.A promotion to a higher position in the: A promotion to a higher position is an advancement, while a layoff is the opposite, a loss of a job.
ww.A firing done because of a worker's thef: Firing because of theft is a termination for cause, based on the employee's own misconduct, unlike a layoff, which is not about conduct.
ww.A paid vacation given to all workers: A paid vacation is time off with pay, which is a benefit, and a layoff is a permanent or temporary end to employment.

rw: The WARN Act generally requires covered employers to give 60 days' advance written notice before mass layoffs or plant closings, so workers can prepare.

ww.A court hearing before any layoffs: The WARN Act does not require a court hearing before layoffs, and its main protection is advance notice to the affected workers and officials.
ww.A full year of paid leave for staff: The WARN Act does not give a year of paid leave, because it only requires notice before large layoffs and plant closings.
ww.Same-day notice given at shift end: Same-day notice at shift end is exactly what the law is meant to prevent, because it requires 60 days of warning for large layoffs.

rw: A hostile work environment exists when harassing or discriminatory conduct is so severe or pervasive that it interferes with an employee's ability to work.

ww.A busy office during a tight monthly dea: A busy office during a deadline is ordinary workplace stress and does not involve harassment based on a protected trait.
ww.A strict manager who is still fair to al: A strict manager who treats everyone fairly is not creating a hostile environment, which requires severe or pervasive harassment or discrimination.
ww.A noisy lunch room at midday for all sta: A noisy lunch room is only an annoyance and has nothing to do with discriminatory conduct that makes a workplace hostile.

rw: Choosing the applicant with the best qualifications for the job is a lawful, merit-based hiring practice that does not rely on protected traits.

ww.Asking applicants about their age or pla: Asking about age or plans for children can lead to discrimination, so such questions are generally improper and unlawful in hiring.
ww.Rejecting applicants because of their na: Rejecting applicants based on national origin or race is illegal discrimination under Title VII, so it is not a lawful hiring practice.
ww.Refusing to hire someone because of thei: Refusing to hire someone because of religion is unlawful discrimination under Title VII, unless an exception such as a BFOQ applies.

rw: A BFOQ is a job requirement based on a characteristic, like sex or religion, that is truly necessary to the business, and it is allowed only in rare cases.

ww.A requirement that any manager is free t: A BFOQ is not a requirement managers can invent, since courts treat it as a narrow exception that must be reasonably necessary to the job.
ww.A way for employers to refuse to hire pe: A BFOQ is not a loophole for refusing groups at will, because it is allowed only when the trait is essential to the work.
ww.A preference for hiring friends and fami: Hiring friends and family is nepotism, which is a preference and not a BFOQ, which must be necessary to the job.

rw: Affirmative action means efforts, such as outreach and recruiting, to widen opportunity for groups that have faced discrimination, within legal limits.

ww.A requirement to hire only the relatives: Affirmative action does not require hiring only relatives of owners, which would be nepotism, and its goal is wider opportunity.
ww.A tax that is charged to large employers: Affirmative action is not a tax, because it is an employment policy for expanding opportunity, not a charge on large employers.
ww.A ban on hiring people from certain grou: Affirmative action does the opposite of banning groups, since its aim is to open doors, not to exclude people from jobs.

rw: Under the FCRA, an employer must give the applicant written notice and get their permission before using a third-party background check report.

ww.A court order that is signed by a federa: A court order is not needed, since the FCRA requires notice and written permission, but no judge has to sign anything for a background check.
ww.Nothing, as background checks are always: Background checks are not allowed without conditions, because the FCRA requires disclosure and consent, and further steps if the report leads to a denial.
ww.Paying the applicant a fee for the full: The employer does not pay the applicant a fee for the report, and the FCRA instead requires clear notice and the applicant's consent.

rw: A payroll deduction is an amount withheld from an employee's gross pay for items such as taxes, insurance premiums or retirement contributions.

ww.A fine that the employer must pay to the: A fine paid by the employer to the state is a penalty and not a deduction, which is an amount taken out of an employee's pay.
ww.An extra bonus that is added to the pay: A bonus adds to pay, while a deduction subtracts from it, so an extra bonus is the opposite of a payroll deduction.
ww.A gift that the company gives to its sta: A gift from the company is not withheld from pay, so it does not fit a deduction, which reduces take-home pay.

rw: Federal income tax withholding is mandatory, because employers are legally required to withhold taxes from wages and send them to the government.

ww.A voluntary retirement plan: A voluntary retirement plan is a deduction the employee chooses, so it is not mandatory, unlike withholding required by law.
ww.A charity donation to a cause: A charity donation is a deduction the employee chooses to give, so it is voluntary, not required by law.
ww.A gym membership at a local club: A gym membership is an optional benefit the employee may pick, so it is a voluntary deduction rather than a mandatory one.

rw: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay that employers may legally pay covered workers, set by federal and state law to protect workers.

ww.The highest hourly pay allowed by law: The highest hourly pay allowed by law would be a wage ceiling, but a minimum wage is the lowest pay allowed.
ww.The wage that is paid to all managers: Managers are usually paid salaries that are set by employers, so the minimum wage is not a pay level for managers only.
ww.A bonus that is given to new hires: A bonus for new hires is an incentive set by the employer, and it is not related to the legal wage floor.

rw: When the state minimum is higher than the federal one, the employer must pay the higher state minimum, since the law more protective of workers applies.

ww.Whichever one is the lower: Following the lower rate would mean paying below the state minimum, which would violate the law, so it is not allowed.
ww.Only the federal minimum rate: Following only the federal minimum would break state law, because employers must follow whichever minimum wage law is more protective for workers.
ww.Neither, as wages are negotiable: Wages are not simply negotiable below the legal minimum, since minimum wage laws set a floor that agreements cannot waive.

rw: Child labor law protects minors from unsafe work and limits their hours so that they can stay in school and stay healthy.

ww.Set the salaries that adults must be pai: Child labor laws do not set adult salaries, because those are covered by minimum wage laws, and child labor laws focus on minors.
ww.Ban all employment for teenagers of ever: Child labor law does not ban all work by teenagers, since it allows age-appropriate jobs with limits on hours and hazards.
ww.Require teenagers to work after school e: Child labor law does not force teenagers to work after school, because it limits work rather than requiring any teenager to work.

rw: Fourteen and fifteen year olds may work only limited hours outside school, such as 3 hours on a school day, and are barred from hazardous jobs.

ww.Unlimited hours at any time of day or ni: Federal rules do not allow unlimited hours at any time, since they limit the hours and times of day that young teens may work.
ww.They may operate dangerous machinery if: Young teens cannot run dangerous machinery even with training, since federal hazardous occupation rules bar work of that kind for minors.
ww.They are not allowed to work at all in a: Fourteen and fifteen year olds are allowed to work in certain jobs under limits, so they are not barred from all employment.

rw: The FLSA does not require meal or rest breaks for adults, though some states require them, and short rest breaks are paid if offered.

ww.Federal law requires a one-hour lunch br: Federal law does not require a one-hour lunch break, because the FLSA does not require meal periods for most workers.
ww.Federal law requires paid vacations for: The FLSA does not require paid vacations, because vacation is a benefit that employers choose to offer, unless a contract provides it.
ww.Federal law bans all breaks during a shi: Federal law does not ban breaks, since employers are free to give them, and some state laws actually require them.

rw: Whistleblower protection laws shield employees who report illegal activity from retaliation, such as firing or demotion, and encourage reporting of wrongdoing.

ww.Stop employees from reporting their conc: Whistleblower laws do the opposite of stopping reports, since they protect employees who report problems so that they can speak up safely.
ww.Reward employees who gossip about others: Whistleblower laws do not reward gossip, since they protect good-faith reports of legal violations, and they are not meant for rumors.
ww.Replace the need for the police entirely: Whistleblower laws do not replace police, as they protect people who report wrongdoing, and the authorities still investigate it.

rw: Being vested means the employee has earned the right to keep the employer's contributions to a retirement plan, usually after a set number of years.

ww.A tax charged on money put in each year: A tax on money put in is not vesting, which instead refers to how much of the employer's contributions an employee has earned.
ww.A fee that is charged by the plan each y: A plan fee is a cost of running the account, whereas vesting is about when employer contributions become the employee's own.
ww.A loan that is taken against the plan: A loan against the plan is a borrowing feature, while vesting refers to ownership of the employer's contributions.

rw: ERISA, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, sets minimum standards for most private retirement and health plans, covering reporting, funding and fiduciary duties.

ww.FLSA: The FLSA governs minimum wage, overtime and child labor, so it does not set standards for private retirement and health plans.
ww.HIPAA: HIPAA protects the privacy and security of health information, and it does not set the broader standards for private retirement plans.
ww.FICA: FICA is the payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare, so it is not the law that regulates private plan standards.

rw: A credit report is a record of a person's borrowing and repayment history, including accounts, balances and late payments, which lenders use to judge risk.

ww.A list of monthly grocery purchases from: A list of grocery purchases is a spending record from stores, and it does not show borrowing and repayment history.
ww.A tax return filed with the government e: A tax return reports income and taxes owed to the government, and it is not a record of credit use.
ww.A statement of the person's employer's p: A statement of an employer's profits is a business financial report, which has nothing to do with a person's credit history.

rw: The FCRA protects the accuracy and privacy of consumer credit information and lets consumers see their reports and dispute errors with the credit bureaus.

ww.Guarantees every consumer a perfect cred: The FCRA does not give anyone a perfect credit score, since it only gives consumers rights over the accuracy of their reports.
ww.Sets the interest rates that banks must: The FCRA does not set interest rates for loans, because banks and the market set rates, and the act deals with credit reporting.
ww.Bans the use of credit cards for travel: The FCRA does not ban credit cards for travel, since it regulates credit reports and not where cards may be used.

rw: Under federal law, consumers can get a free credit report from each major bureau at least once a year at annualcreditreport.com.

ww.Only after two denials: Free reports are not limited to those who were denied credit, because every consumer can get one each year, and denials give extra rights.
ww.Once every ten years: Waiting ten years is far longer than the law requires, since consumers can request a free report once a year, or more often in some cases.
ww.Never; each costs money: Credit reports are not always sold, since federal law gives every consumer a free copy at least once a year from each bureau.

rw: TILA requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the APR and finance charges, so borrowers can compare loan offers and understand the total cost.

ww.The credit scores of the borrower's frie: TILA does not require disclosure of the credit scores of the borrower's friends or family, because it deals with the lender's terms.
ww.The salaries that the lender pays its em: Lender employee salaries are internal business information, and TILA does not require them to be disclosed to borrowers.
ww.The lender's own internal profit goals f: A lender's internal profit goals are private business plans, while TILA requires clear disclosure of the loan's costs to the borrower.
